components.text: It contests the inference from some inconsistencies to historical unreliability by distinguishing reliability from inerrancy and requiring counterbalancing errors.
Whether important alleged errors outweigh the conceded accurate outline and other verifiable claims.
It argues that conceded and asserted Gospel accuracy outweighs the limited alleged errors and therefore defeats the broad unreliability inference.
It classifies the challenged birth material as intermediate or lesser rather than motion-defeating.
It classifies the challenged resurrection details as below the shared major claim.
It includes Jesus' teachings among matters to be weighed against the wider accurate record.
Whether the alleged errors are numerous and important enough to defeat the conceded accurate Gospel core.
It identifies the pro balance's allegedly false classification of birth, resurrection, and self-presentation disputes as nonmajor and states that this defeats the cumulative inference.
It accepts weighing in principle but argues that the disputed examples occupy the major rather than lesser side of that standard.
Whether Ehrman’s examples are merely intermediate or lesser and therefore outweighed by cumulative agreement.
How the proposed spectrum should weight errors concerning central narratives and teachings.
It answers that all four Gospels share the major resurrection claim and classifies their surrounding differences as lesser matters.
It directly disputes the con classification of the resurrection disagreement as a major-claim conflict.
Whether narrative differences negate the shared major claim that Jesus was resurrected.
Whether resurrection disagreements concern the major claim itself or surrounding matters.
It offers a general approximation principle but does not apply that principle to the decisive reporting, movement, or location conflicts identified in the target.
It supplies contrary material suggesting that some apparent errors result from inappropriate modern precision demands.
Whether the specific alleged inconsistencies and nonhistorical accounts are substantial enough to establish unreliability.
It proposes that Joseph had property connections in both Bethlehem and Nazareth, supplying a possible reconciliation of the original-home conflict.
The proposed reconciliation challenges the classification of the birth discrepancy as an established major error.
Whether Matthew and Luke require incompatible original homes and movements for Joseph’s family.
It attacks the reconciliation's dual-property premise by invoking the hand-to-mouth economics of workers like Joseph and states that such people lacked multiple residences.
By challenging the offered birth reconciliation, it preserves the alleged error's place in the cumulative balance.
Whether a low-income manual laborer plausibly maintained property or residences in both Bethlehem and Nazareth.
It presses the unresolved Luke-versus-Galilee movement question that remains despite agreement on the broad resurrection claim.
The concrete forty-day Jerusalem chronology tests whether the generic approximation principle can explain the discrepancy.
The question challenges treating the location and movement conflict as merely lesser material.
Whether shared affirmation of resurrection resolves the concrete conflict over the disciples’ post-resurrection movements.
It answers with a Jerusalem-to-Galilee sequence drawn from John and argues that Luke merely omits the Galilee stage.
It supplies a composite sequence intended to reconcile the earlier location conflict.
A compatible sequence would remove this resurrection-location example from the alleged major-error balance.
Whether Luke’s Jerusalem material and Matthew’s Galilee material can fit one post-resurrection chronology.
Whether the Jerusalem and Galilee appearance traditions require mutually exclusive locations.
It argues that ancient compositional latitude included invented or reconstructed speeches, so a generic gist convention cannot guarantee historical accuracy.
It challenges the evidential trust assigned to ancient biographical reporting under the proposed reliability standard.
It introduces composition and non-eyewitness distance as contrary considerations in the cumulative balance.
It does not address the specific Jerusalem-Galilee sequence.
Whether approximate ancient reporting can still preserve an accurate gist in the disputed Gospel material.
Whether the specific resurrection sequence is supported rather than harmonistically constructed.
It denies a long telephone chain and proposes named eyewitness-linked source routes through Peter, Mark, Luke's sources, and John.
The claimed eyewitness basis for John supplies contrary source-proximity material but does not answer the earlier-source silence inference.
The proposed transmission route supplies positive support against the governing unreliability thesis.
Whether decades of transmission and non-eyewitness composition make the Gospel tradition comparable to unreliable invented speech.
Whether John lacks adequate proximity to eyewitness testimony.
Whether alleged nonhistorical material defeats the reliability of the transmitted Gospel core.
It supplies allegedly comparable Synoptic material by reading Mark's trial scene and Daniel 7 as an indirect claim to divine identity.
Earlier Synoptic divine-identity material would reduce dependence on John's later speech reporting.
Whether earlier Synoptic material contains claims comparable enough to John’s divine self-presentation to establish continuity.
Whether a disputed saying can be historically credited rather than treated as later biographical composition.
It identifies the missing self-reference premise: Mark says the hearers will see the Son of Man rather than explicitly saying Jesus is that figure.
It preserves a material discontinuity in self-presentation despite the broader cumulative-reliability claim.
Whether Mark 14 explicitly identifies Jesus with the coming Son of Man and thereby establishes a divine self-claim.
It argues that evangelists changed inherited material for theological messages, challenging the inference from motivated transmission to historical accuracy.
It accepts ancient compositional difference but disputes that accurate historical gist was the authors' controlling priority.
Its general reshaping account supplies a possible explanation for divergent Christological presentations.
Whether motivated Gospel transmission primarily preserved historical gist rather than reshaping inherited material for theological purposes.
Whether differences are best explained as permissible approximation rather than message-driven alteration.
It offers a remembered-source explanation for Luke's infancy material, contrary to treating its distinctiveness solely as theological alteration.
The proposed Marian provenance supports one account's source proximity but does not reconcile its sequence with Matthew.
A family-memory source would provide an alternative to authorial invention for the infancy material.
Whether Luke’s infancy material lacks a plausible remembered source close to the reported family events.
Whether a Marian source resolves the substantive chronological incompatibility between Matthew and Luke.
Whether theological composition better explains Luke’s infancy traditions than preserved family memory.
